questions.subtopic: UN Charter: prohibition on use of force
questions.stem: Under Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which conduct must Member States generally refrain from in their international relations?
options: Threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state
Any economic sanction approved by a regional organisation
All criticism of another state's domestic policy
Any diplomatic negotiation involving a disputed border
explanations: Correct. Article 2(4) requires Members to refrain from the threat or use of force against a state's territorial integrity or political independence, or otherwise inconsistently with UN purposes.
The Charter does not prohibit every economic sanction; sanctions may be authorised under Chapter VII.

Negotiation over a disputed border is not prohibited; peaceful settlement is encouraged.

questions.subtopic: International Court of Justice: contentious jurisdiction
questions.stem: Two states submit a contentious dispute to the International Court of Justice. Which statement best describes the legal basis of the Court's jurisdiction in such a case?
options: The Court has compulsory jurisdiction over every dispute between UN members
Jurisdiction generally depends on the consent of the states concerned
The UN General Assembly must approve every judgment before it becomes binding
Any private company may independently file a contentious case against a state
explanations: ICJ jurisdiction is not automatically compulsory for every dispute between all UN members.
Correct. In contentious cases, the Court's jurisdiction rests on state consent, which may be expressed through a special agreement, treaty clause or optional-clause declarations.
The General Assembly does not approve ICJ judgments; judgments in contentious cases bind the parties to that case.
Private companies are not parties entitled to institute contentious proceedings before the ICJ.

questions.subtopic: Photoelectric effect: intensity and kinetic energy
questions.stem: Light of a fixed frequency above the threshold frequency shines on a clean metal surface. If only the light intensity is increased, what happens in the ideal photoelectric-effect model?
options: Maximum kinetic energy increases, but the number of emitted electrons stays fixed
Maximum kinetic energy remains fixed, while the emission rate can increase
Threshold frequency decreases
Work function of the metal increases
explanations: At fixed frequency, increasing intensity does not increase the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons.
Correct. Greater intensity supplies more photons per unit time, so the photoelectron emission rate can increase, while maximum kinetic energy remains set by frequency.
Threshold frequency is a material property determined by work function; intensity does not lower it.
The work function is a property of the metal surface and is not increased merely by changing incident intensity.

A catalyst accelerates both directions; it does not shift the equilibrium composition by itself.
Correct. By lowering activation barriers for forward and reverse pathways, a catalyst helps the system attain equilibrium faster without changing K.
A catalyst changes reaction rates, not the reaction enthalpy of the initial and final states.

questions.stem: Why can chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) cause catalytic depletion of stratospheric ozone after reaching the upper atmosphere?
options: They release chlorine radicals under ultraviolet radiation, and those radicals can participate in repeated ozone-destroying cycles
They convert all atmospheric oxygen directly into carbon dioxide
They absorb only infrared radiation and therefore cool the stratosphere
They increase the rate of nitrogen fixation in the stratosphere
explanations: Correct. UV photolysis of CFCs can release chlorine radicals; catalytic cycles allow a chlorine radical to destroy many ozone molecules before being deactivated.
CFC photochemistry does not convert atmospheric oxygen into carbon dioxide.
CFC-driven ozone depletion is not explained by infrared absorption cooling the stratosphere.
Nitrogen fixation is not the mechanism of CFC-related ozone loss.

questions.stem: Which feature characterises the Bhabar belt along the Himalayan foothills?
options: Fine alluvium deposited in a deltaic estuary
A porous belt of coarse pebbles and sediments in which streams may disappear underground
A permanently waterlogged marsh belt south of the Terai
A high-altitude zone of glacial cirques
explanations: A deltaic estuary is not the Bhabar belt.
Correct. The Bhabar is a narrow, coarse, porous depositional belt at the foothills where streams can sink into the permeable deposits.
The marshy belt where streams re-emerge is the Terai, not Bhabar.
Glacial cirques are high-mountain landforms, not the foothill Bhabar belt.

questions.stem: Which comparison between the Eastern Ghats and Western Ghats is geographically most accurate?
options: Both ranges form equally continuous escarpments along the coast
The Eastern Ghats are more discontinuous because major east-flowing rivers dissect them, whereas the Western Ghats are comparatively continuous
The Western Ghats are lower and more discontinuous than the Eastern Ghats throughout their length
The Eastern Ghats are a young fold mountain system formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
explanations: The two ranges do not have equal continuity; the Eastern Ghats are notably discontinuous.
Correct. Large rivers such as the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri cut across the Eastern Ghats, while the Western Ghats form a more continuous escarpment.

The Eastern Ghats are an ancient eroded range, not a young Himalayan-style fold system.

A martial dance performed exclusively by Kakatiya soldiers
A Buddhist monastic ceremony held at Phanigiri
explanations: Bathukamma is not a boat race.
Correct. Bathukamma is a floral festival centred on seasonal flowers, community singing and collective celebration by women.
The martial dance association is closer to Perini Sivatandavam, not Bathukamma.
Phanigiri is an archaeological Buddhist site; Bathukamma is not a monastic ceremony.

70 litres per capita per day
100 litres per capita per day
150 litres per capita per day
explanations: 55 LPCD is not the rural service norm in the Mission Bhagiratha description.
70 LPCD is not the stated rural target.

150 LPCD is the stated norm for municipal corporations, not rural households.

Deepening only major river channels and constructing coastal ports
Replacing all minor irrigation tanks with groundwater borewells
Lining every village road and installing rooftop solar panels

Road construction and rooftop solar installation are not the defining Mission Kakatiya works.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes Telangana's Rythu Bima from an agricultural crop-insurance scheme?

It is a group life-insurance scheme that provides a death benefit to the enrolled farmer's nominee
It is a loan-waiver programme for all rural households

Electricity reimbursement is not the benefit described for Rythu Bima.

questions.topic: Logical Reasoning; Analytical Ability and Data Interpretation
questions.stem: A treatment operator mixes 120 litres of water containing a dissolved tracer at 30 mg/L with 80 litres containing the same tracer at 10 mg/L. Assuming volumes are additive and no tracer is lost, what is the final concentration?
options: 18 mg/L
20 mg/L
22 mg/L
24 mg/L
explanations: 18 mg/L would correspond to a different weighted total; the tracer mass is 3,600 + 800 = 4,400 mg.
20 mg/L is the unweighted mean of the two concentrations and ignores the unequal volumes.
Correct. Final concentration = (120×30 + 80×10)/(120+80) = 4,400/200 = 22 mg/L.
24 mg/L is not obtained from the conserved tracer mass divided by the total volume.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Logical Reasoning; Analytical Ability and Data Interpretation; weighted-average concentration calculation, based on conservation of solute mass.

questions.topic: Logical Reasoning; Analytical Ability and Data Interpretation
questions.subtopic: Pipes and cisterns: two inlets and one outlet
questions.stem: In a test tank, inlet A fills the tank in 12 hours, inlet B fills it in 18 hours, and an outlet empties a full tank in 36 hours. If all three operate together from empty, how long will the tank take to fill?
options: 6 hours
8 hours
9 hours
12 hours
explanations: Six hours would require a net rate of one-sixth tank per hour, greater than the actual net rate.
Eight hours is not consistent with the combined rates.
Correct. Net rate = 1/12 + 1/18 − 1/36 = 4/36 = 1/9 tank per hour, so the tank fills in 9 hours.
Twelve hours ignores the positive contribution of inlet B and the outlet's smaller emptying rate.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Logical Reasoning; Analytical Ability and Data Interpretation; work-rate and combined-efficiency problem.

questions.topic: Logical Reasoning; Analytical Ability and Data Interpretation
questions.stem: A water utility reduces non-revenue water from 25% of system input to 20%, with input volume unchanged at 40 million litres per day. By what percentage has the volume of non-revenue water fallen relative to its original volume?
explanations: Five percentage points is the absolute reduction in the share, not the percentage fall relative to the original loss volume.
15% is not obtained by comparing 10 with the original 25.
Correct. Original loss is 0.25×40 = 10 MLD; new loss is 0.20×40 = 8 MLD. The reduction is 2/10 = 20%.
25% would be the reduction only if the loss fell from 10 to 7.5 MLD.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Logical Reasoning; Analytical Ability and Data Interpretation; percentage change and water-loss interpretation.

questions.stem: Choose the grammatically correct completion: 'If the isolation valve ___ before the pump started, the tank ___ overflowed.'
options: was closed; will not have
had been closed; would not have
would be closed; had not
has closed; would not
explanations: 'Was closed; will not have' mixes an unsuitable past condition with a future-perfect result.
Correct. The third conditional uses past perfect in the if-clause ('had been closed') and 'would have' plus past participle in the result clause.
'Would be closed; had not' reverses the clause structure and does not form the required conditional.
'Has closed; would not' mixes present perfect with an incomplete conditional result.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Basic English (10th class Standard); standard English grammar reference, third conditional / unreal past condition.

questions.subtopic: English usage: discuss versus discuss about
questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses the verb 'discuss' correctly in standard formal English.
options: The engineers discussed about the leakage report.
The engineers discussed the leakage report during the meeting.
The engineers discussed on the leakage report during the meeting.
The engineers discussed regarding the leakage report.
explanations: 'Discuss about' is redundant in standard usage because 'discuss' takes a direct object.
Correct. 'Discussed the leakage report' uses the verb with its direct object.
'Discussed on' is not the standard transitive construction in this sentence.
'Discussed regarding' is also an incorrect or needlessly redundant construction here.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Basic English (10th class Standard); Oxford Learner's Dictionaries / standard transitive verb usage for 'discuss'; https://www.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/

questions.stem: A random variable X has mean 20 and variance 9. Using Chebyshev's inequality, what is the largest guaranteed upper bound on P(|X−20| ≥ 6)?
explanations: 1/2 is a weaker bound than the inequality gives for this deviation.
1/3 is also larger than the Chebyshev bound.
Correct. Chebyshev gives P(|X−μ|≥a) ≤ σ²/a² = 9/36 = 1/4.
1/9 would require a deviation of three standard deviations, not two.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; Sheldon Ross, A First Course in Probability, Chebyshev inequality; https://www.pearson.com/

questions.subtopic: Sampling distribution of the sample mean
questions.stem: A population has variance 16. A simple random sample of 25 independent observations is drawn. What is the variance of the sample mean, assuming sampling with replacement or an effectively infinite population?
explanations: 16 is the population variance, not the variance of the mean of 25 independent observations.
4 is the population standard deviation, not the required variance.
Correct. Var(X̄)=σ²/n=16/25=0.64 under the stated independence assumption.
0.16 would incorrectly divide the variance by 100.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; Ross, A First Course in Probability, sampling distributions and variance of the sample mean.

questions.stem: The lifetime T of a component follows an exponential distribution with mean 5 hours. Given that it has already operated for 3 hours, what is the probability that it operates for at least 5 additional hours?
options: e⁻⁵
e⁻¹
1−e⁻¹
e⁻⁸⁄⁵
explanations: e⁻⁵ would correspond to a five-hour interval at rate 1 per hour, not rate 1/5 per hour.
Correct. The exponential distribution is memoryless: P(T>8 | T>3)=P(T>5)=e^(−5/5)=e⁻¹.
1−e⁻¹ is the probability of failure within the next five hours, not survival for at least five hours.
e⁻⁸⁄⁵ is the probability of surviving eight hours from the start, not five additional hours conditional on surviving three.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; Ross, A First Course in Probability, exponential distribution and memoryless property.

questions.stem: If the number of service interruptions in a fixed interval follows a Poisson distribution with parameter λ=2, what is the probability of observing no interruptions in that interval?
options: 2e⁻²
e⁻²
1−e⁻²
2e⁻¹
explanations: 2e⁻² is the probability of exactly one event, not zero.
Correct. For X~Poisson(2), P(X=0)=e⁻²·2⁰/0!=e⁻².
1−e⁻² is the probability of at least one event.
2e⁻¹ is not the Poisson probability mass at zero for λ=2.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; Ross, A First Course in Probability, Poisson distribution.

questions.stem: Let A contain 3 distinct elements and B contain 5 distinct elements. How many one-to-one functions f:A→B are possible?
explanations: 15 counts 3×5 only if assignments are not distinguished correctly across all domain elements.
30 omits one factor in the falling factorial count.
Correct. The images of the three distinct elements must be distinct: 5×4×3=60 injective functions.
125=5³ counts all functions, including those that map different elements of A to the same element of B.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Set Theory & Algebra; Linear Algebra; Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, functions and one-to-one mappings.

questions.stem: A square matrix A satisfies A²=A. Which set contains every possible eigenvalue of A over the complex numbers?
options: Only {−1,1}
Only {0,1}
All non-zero real numbers
All complex roots of unity
explanations: An eigenvalue of −1 would require 1=−1 after applying A²=A to an eigenvector, which is impossible.
Correct. If Av=λv, then A²v=λ²v and Av=λv; hence λ²=λ, so λ(λ−1)=0 and λ is 0 or 1.
The equation restricts eigenvalues to two values, not arbitrary non-zero reals.
Roots of unity other than 1 do not generally satisfy λ²=λ.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Set Theory & Algebra; Linear Algebra; Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, eigenvalues and idempotent linear operators.

questions.subtopic: Orthogonality of eigenvectors of symmetric matrices
questions.stem: For a real symmetric matrix, eigenvectors corresponding to two distinct eigenvalues are necessarily:
options: Linearly dependent
Orthogonal under the usual inner product
Equal in magnitude component by component
Both eigenvalues necessarily zero
explanations: Eigenvectors associated with distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, not dependent.
Correct. Real symmetric matrices are self-adjoint; eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
There is no requirement that their components have equal magnitudes.
A real symmetric matrix may have non-zero eigenvalues; the statement concerns eigenvectors, not zero eigenvalues.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Set Theory & Algebra; Linear Algebra; standard spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices, e.g. Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right.

questions.stem: A real symmetric matrix A is positive definite if xᵀAx>0 for every non-zero real vector x. Which statement about its eigenvalues is necessarily true?
options: All eigenvalues are strictly positive
All eigenvalues are non-positive
At least one eigenvalue must be zero
Eigenvalues may be non-real
explanations: Correct. For a real symmetric matrix, positive definiteness is equivalent to all eigenvalues being strictly positive.
Non-positive eigenvalues would violate xᵀAx>0 for an eigenvector associated with such an eigenvalue.
A zero eigenvalue would make the quadratic form zero for a non-zero eigenvector, contradicting positive definiteness.
Real symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues by the spectral theorem.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Set Theory & Algebra; Linear Algebra; standard spectral theorem and positive-definite matrices, e.g. Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right.

questions.topic: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic
questions.subtopic: Maximum independent set in a path graph
questions.stem: For the path graph P₅ with vertices v₁–v₂–v₃–v₄–v₅, what is the size of a maximum independent set?
explanations: Two vertices can be selected, but the set {v₁,v₃,v₅} shows that a larger independent set exists.
Correct. Choosing v₁, v₃ and v₅ gives three vertices with no edge between any pair; no four vertices can be selected without including adjacent vertices in P₅.
Any selection of four of the five path vertices must include at least one adjacent pair, so it is not independent.
All five vertices cannot be selected because each consecutive pair is connected by an edge.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; standard definition of independent sets and path graphs, e.g. West, Introduction to Graph Theory.

questions.topic: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic
questions.subtopic: Combinatorics: binary strings with fixed Hamming weight
questions.stem: An 8-bit status word must contain exactly three bits set to 1. How many different bit patterns satisfy this requirement?
explanations: 28 is not the number of ways to choose three distinct bit positions from eight.
Correct. Choose which three of the eight positions contain 1: C(8,3)=8×7×6/(3×2×1)=56.
64 counts all patterns of length six, not 8-bit patterns with exactly three ones.
70 is C(8,4), the number of patterns with exactly four ones.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, combinations and binomial coefficients.

questions.topic: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic
questions.stem: Which condition is equivalent to an undirected graph being bipartite?
options: It contains at least one Hamiltonian cycle
It contains no cycle of any length
It contains no cycle of odd length
Every vertex has even degree
explanations: A bipartite graph need not contain a Hamiltonian cycle.
A bipartite graph may contain even cycles, so it need not be acyclic.
Correct. An undirected graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle.
Even degrees at all vertices do not guarantee bipartiteness; for example, K₃ has all degrees 2 but is not bipartite.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; standard characterisation of bipartite graphs, e.g. West, Introduction to Graph Theory.

questions.topic: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic
questions.subtopic: Hasse diagrams of partially ordered sets
questions.stem: When drawing a Hasse diagram for a finite partially ordered set, which relations are conventionally omitted from the diagram?
options: Cover relations between comparable elements
Reflexive loops and transitive relations implied by other paths
All relations involving maximal elements
All relations between incomparable elements
explanations: Cover relations are the essential edges shown in a Hasse diagram.
Correct. Reflexive loops are omitted, and a relation implied by transitivity through an intermediate element is not drawn as a separate edge.
Maximal elements are represented as vertices and are not removed from the diagram.
Incomparable pairs have no order relation to draw; their absence is not the rule being asked about.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Mathematical Logic; Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, partially ordered sets and Hasse diagrams.

questions.subtopic: Sequential circuit timing: minimum clock period
questions.stem: A register-to-register path has clock-to-Q delay 0.6 ns, combinational delay 2.1 ns and setup time 0.3 ns. Ignoring skew and uncertainty, what is the minimum clock period required for correct capture?
options: 2.1 ns
2.7 ns
3.0 ns
3.6 ns
explanations: 2.1 ns omits both the launch register's clock-to-Q delay and the capture register's setup requirement.
2.7 ns includes clock-to-Q and combinational delay but omits setup time.
Correct. The minimum period is tCQ + tcomb + tsetup = 0.6 + 2.1 + 0.3 = 3.0 ns.
3.6 ns adds an extra 0.6 ns not required by the stated path model.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; sequential-circuit timing and setup constraints; Mano, Digital Design, sequential circuit timing.

questions.stem: In 8-bit signed two's-complement arithmetic, the bit patterns for +100 and +60 are added. What result is stored, and what is the status of the operation?
options: −96 with signed overflow
+160 with no overflow
−96 with no overflow
+32 with signed overflow
explanations: Correct. 100+60=160; modulo 256 the stored byte is 1010 0000, which represents −96 in 8-bit two's complement. Since two positive operands produce a negative result, signed overflow occurred.
+160 is outside the representable range −128 to +127, so it cannot be represented without overflow in 8 bits.
The stored pattern represents −96, but the operation does overflow because the mathematical result is outside the signed range.
+32 is not the modulo-256 sum of the two operands.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; number representation and computer arithmetic; Mano, Computer System Architecture, signed binary arithmetic.

questions.stem: Two valid packed-BCD digits, 8 and 7, are added. After the required BCD correction, what packed-BCD result represents the decimal sum?
explanations: 0000 1111 is the uncorrected binary sum 15, not a valid single BCD digit representation.
Correct. 8+7=15; the BCD result is tens digit 0001 and units digit 0101, i.e. 0001 0101.
0001 0001 represents decimal 11 in packed BCD.
0000 1001 represents decimal 9, not 15.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; computer arithmetic and BCD addition; Mano, Digital Design, number codes and arithmetic circuits.

questions.stem: A 4-to-1 multiplexer uses A as the most significant select input and B as the least significant select input. Which data-input assignment implements F=A⊕B?
options: D₀=0, D₁=1, D₂=1, D₃=0
D₀=1, D₁=0, D₂=0, D₃=1
D₀=0, D₁=0, D₂=1, D₃=1
D₀=1, D₁=1, D₂=0, D₃=0
explanations: Correct. For select AB=00,01,10,11, XOR outputs 0,1,1,0 respectively, so the four data inputs must match that sequence.
This assignment implements XNOR, the complement of XOR.
This assignment produces F=A, not XOR.
This assignment produces F=¬A, not XOR.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; combinational circuit synthesis using multiplexers; Mano, Digital Design, multiplexers and Boolean functions.

questions.stem: A byte-addressable 32-bit machine has a 32 KiB, two-way set-associative cache with 64-byte blocks. Assuming conventional indexing, how many tag bits are in a physical address?
explanations: Sixteen bits would leave too many bits assigned to the set index or block offset.
Correct. There are 32 KiB/64 B=512 blocks and 512/2=256 sets, so offset=6 bits, index=8 bits and tag=32−6−8=18 bits.
Twenty bits would result from using an incorrect smaller index or offset field.
Twenty-two bits would undercount the number of address bits needed for the set and byte offset.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; cache organisation and address fields; Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, cache mapping.

questions.stem: An ideal five-stage pipeline has a one-cycle stage latency and no stalls. How many clock cycles are required to complete 100 instructions after the pipeline is filled?
explanations: 100 cycles would be the ideal count only if the pipeline had one stage.
Correct. An ideal k-stage pipeline needs k+n−1 cycles; 5+100−1=104 cycles.
500 cycles corresponds to executing every instruction through all five stages serially without overlap.
505 cycles incorrectly adds a full pipeline latency after every instruction.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; instruction pipelining and throughput; Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, pipelined datapaths.

questions.stem: In cycle-stealing Direct Memory Access, how does the DMA controller typically obtain the system bus?
options: It disables the CPU permanently for the entire I/O transfer
It takes individual bus cycles when required, temporarily delaying CPU memory access
It copies data only through CPU registers and never becomes bus master
It interrupts the CPU after every byte and requires software to copy that byte
explanations: Cycle stealing does not permanently disable the CPU for the entire transfer.
Correct. The DMA controller temporarily takes individual bus cycles; CPU memory accesses may be delayed during those cycles.
DMA is specifically intended to transfer data without requiring the CPU to copy every word through its registers.
Per-byte software copying describes programmed I/O rather than cycle-stealing DMA.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; I/O interface and DMA mode; Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, I/O and DMA.

questions.stem: In a conventional PC-relative addressing mode, the effective address is formed by which operation?
options: Adding a sign-extended displacement to the program counter (or the architecture-defined next-PC base)
Multiplying the displacement by the contents of the stack pointer
Using the displacement as an absolute physical address without modification
Adding the contents of the accumulator to the memory data bus
explanations: Correct. PC-relative addressing adds a signed displacement to a program-counter base, with the precise base (current or next instruction) defined by the architecture.
The stack pointer is not the base register in PC-relative addressing.
An absolute address uses the address field directly; PC-relative mode applies a PC-based offset.
The accumulator and memory data bus do not define PC-relative effective-address calculation.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; machine instructions and addressing modes; Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, addressing modes.

questions.subtopic: C recursion with a static local variable
questions.stem: Consider the C function `int f(int n){ static int x=0; if(n==0) return 0; x++; int y=f(n-1); return y+x; }`. What does `f(3)` return when called once in a fresh program execution?
explanations: The three non-base calls increment the shared static x to 3; each call then returns the recursive result plus the current x, producing 3, 6 and finally 9.
Six would result if only two increments were added during unwinding.
Correct. x becomes 1, then 2, then 3 before the base case returns; each of the three pending calls adds 3, giving 9.
Twelve would require four additions of 3, but only three non-base invocations occur.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; C functions, recursion and storage duration; ISO C draft N1570, storage duration and block-scope static objects; https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

questions.stem: Which C declaration defines `fp` as a pointer to a function taking two `int` arguments and returning an `int`?
options: int (*fp)(int, int);
int *(*fp)(int, int);
int (*fp)(int);
int (*fp)(int, int, int);
explanations: Correct. The parentheses bind `*fp` as a pointer declarator; the pointed-to function accepts two int arguments and returns int.
This declares fp as a pointer to a function that returns a pointer to int, not a function returning int.
This is a pointer to a function taking one int argument, so the parameter list is wrong.
This is a pointer to a function taking three int arguments, so the parameter list is wrong.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; C programming, declarators and function pointers; ISO C draft N1570, declarators; https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

questions.stem: In C, `strncpy(dest, src, n)` is called with `src` containing at least n non-null characters. Which statement is correct about the resulting destination array?
options: It is guaranteed to end with a null character
It contains exactly n characters and is always a valid C string
It may contain no terminating null character within the first n bytes
The function appends a null character after byte n in all cases
explanations: A null terminator is not guaranteed when the source length is at least n.
The copied bytes need not include a terminator, so the result is not always a valid C string.
Correct. `strncpy` pads with null bytes only when the source is shorter than n; if at least n non-null characters are copied, no null terminator is appended within those n bytes.
The function does not automatically write an extra byte after the n-byte destination region.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; C strings and standard library; ISO C draft N1570, §7.24.2.4 strncpy; https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

questions.stem: A binary max-heap containing n elements is stored in an array. What is the worst-case time complexity of inserting one new key?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
explanations: O(1) is the best case when the new key remains at the leaf, not the worst case.
Correct. After insertion at the next leaf position, the key may move up at most the height of the heap, which is O(log n).
O(n) is not required because the heap property can be restored by following one rootward path.
O(n log n) would be unnecessarily high; insertion does not rebuild the entire heap.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; binary heaps; CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, priority queues and heap operations.

questions.subtopic: Kahn's topological sorting and cycle detection
questions.stem: Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting of a directed graph removes zero-indegree vertices repeatedly. If fewer than V vertices are output, what can be concluded?
options: The graph is necessarily a complete directed graph
The graph contains at least one directed cycle
The graph is disconnected but acyclic
Every vertex has indegree exactly one
explanations: A complete directed graph is not the specific condition detected by Kahn's algorithm.
Correct. If fewer than V vertices can be removed, the remaining subgraph has no zero-indegree vertex and therefore contains a directed cycle.
Disconnected acyclic directed graphs can still have all vertices output in a topological order.
The algorithm does not imply that every vertex has indegree one.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; graph traversal and topological sorting; CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, topological sort.

questions.stem: A depth-first search is run once over every vertex of a graph represented by adjacency lists. What is its time complexity in terms of V vertices and E edges?
options: O(V²) for every graph representation
O(V+E)
O(E log V)
O(VE)
explanations: O(V²) is the usual bound for an adjacency-matrix scan, not adjacency lists.
Correct. Each vertex is visited once and each adjacency-list edge is examined a constant number of times, giving O(V+E).
Sorting edges is not part of standard DFS.
O(VE) overstates the work for adjacency-list DFS.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; graph traversals and complexity analysis; CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, depth-first search.

questions.stem: Which complexity statement is correct for in-place heapsort on an array of n elements?
options: Worst-case O(n log n) time and O(1) auxiliary array space
Worst-case O(n²) time and O(log n) auxiliary array space
Worst-case O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary array space
Worst-case O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary array space
explanations: Correct. Building a heap takes O(n), and n extract operations take O(n log n); the in-place array implementation uses O(1) auxiliary space.
O(n²) is not the worst-case running time of heapsort.
An additional O(n) array is not required by in-place heapsort.
O(log n) is too small for sorting n arbitrary keys under the comparison model.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; sorting and best/worst-case time/space analysis; CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, heapsort.

questions.stem: In the stable version of counting sort, after cumulative counts have been computed, why is the input array normally traversed from right to left when placing elements into the output array?
options: It makes the algorithm comparison-based
It preserves the relative order of records with equal keys
It reduces the key range k to log k
It guarantees that the output is sorted even if cumulative counts are omitted
explanations: Counting sort remains a non-comparison sorting algorithm; traversal direction does not make it comparison-based.
Correct. Placing items from right to left while decrementing cumulative positions preserves the original relative order of equal-key records.
The key range k is not changed by the traversal direction.
Cumulative counts are required to determine final positions; reversing traversal does not replace them.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; sorting and stability; CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, Counting Sort.

questions.stem: In the subset construction for converting an ε-NFA to a DFA, what does ε-closure(q) contain?
options: Only q, with no other states
Every state reachable from q using one or more input symbols
q itself and every state reachable from q using zero or more ε-transitions
Only accepting states reachable from q by ε-transitions
explanations: The zero-transition path means q itself is always included, but ε-closure may contain additional states.
Input-symbol transitions are not ε-transitions and are not included in ε-closure.
Correct. ε-closure includes q and all states reachable by any finite sequence of ε-transitions, including a sequence of length zero.
ε-closure is not restricted to accepting states; it includes all states reachable through ε-transitions.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; finite automata and ε-NFA conversion; Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, subset construction.

questions.stem: A standard way to decide whether two complete DFAs accept exactly the same language is to construct a product automaton for their symmetric difference. What must be tested in that product automaton?
options: Whether it has any reachable accepting state where exactly one component state is accepting
Whether both initial states are accepting
Whether every product state has two outgoing transitions
Whether the two DFAs have the same number of states
explanations: Correct. The symmetric-difference automaton accepts strings accepted by exactly one DFA; the languages are equivalent precisely when no accepting product state is reachable.
Initial-state acceptance alone cannot establish equivalence for all strings.
The number of outgoing transitions depends on the alphabet and completeness; it is not the equivalence criterion.
Equivalent DFAs may have different numbers of states before minimisation.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; finite automata and language equivalence; Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, closure and decision properties of regular languages.

questions.stem: An NFA has n states. Under the standard subset construction, what is the maximum possible number of states in an equivalent DFA before minimisation?
options: n
n squared
2 times n
2 to the power n
explanations: The construction can require more states than n because each DFA state represents a subset of NFA states.
n² is not the general upper bound for the subset construction.
2n is not the number of all subsets of an n-element state set.
Correct. An n-state NFA has 2ⁿ possible subsets of states, so the constructed DFA has at most 2ⁿ states.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; finite automata and NFA-to-DFA conversion; Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, subset construction.

questions.stem: During intermediate-code generation for a conditional branch, the target label of a jump is not yet known. What is the purpose of backpatching?
options: To fill the unresolved jump target later, when its address or label becomes known
To allocate a new register for every Boolean variable
To eliminate all branches by converting them into data declarations
To perform lexical analysis on the source file a second time
explanations: Correct. Backpatching records incomplete jump instructions and fills their target addresses once the relevant labels are determined during code generation.
Register allocation is a separate optimisation/task and is not the purpose of backpatching.
Backpatching does not eliminate control-flow branches or convert them into declarations.
Lexical analysis is not repeated to resolve an unknown branch target.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Compiler Design; syntax-directed translation and intermediate-code generation; Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, backpatching and Boolean expressions.

questions.subtopic: Abstract syntax tree versus parse tree
questions.stem: Compared with a concrete parse tree, an abstract syntax tree (AST) normally:
options: Retains every grammar punctuation token and every intermediate nonterminal
Omits syntactic details that are not needed for the program's essential structure
Represents only lexical tokens and no operators
Must contain more nodes than the corresponding parse tree
explanations: A concrete parse tree usually preserves grammar productions and punctuation more explicitly than an AST.
Correct. An AST removes grammar-only structure such as redundant parentheses and punctuation while retaining meaningful constructs and relationships.
An AST represents operators, expressions and statements, not merely lexical tokens.
An AST is generally more compact; it need not and normally does not contain more nodes than a parse tree.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Compiler Design; syntax trees and intermediate representations; Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, syntax trees.

questions.stem: In a conventional stack-based runtime environment, what does the dynamic link (control link) in an activation record normally identify?
options: The activation record of the lexically enclosing procedure
The activation record of the caller procedure
The address of the first instruction in the current function
The global symbol table
explanations: The lexically enclosing procedure is normally associated with a static link, not the dynamic link.
Correct. The dynamic/control link points to the caller's activation record and supports restoration of the caller's environment.
The return address identifies where execution resumes; it is not the dynamic link itself.
The global symbol table is not the activation record's dynamic link.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Compiler Design; runtime environments and activation records; Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, runtime storage organisation.

questions.stem: Within a conventional multithreaded process, which resource is normally private to each thread rather than shared by all threads of that process?
options: The process's code segment
The process's global data and heap
The thread's stack and register context
The process's open-file table
explanations: Threads of one process normally share the process code address space.
Global data and heap are normally shared by threads in the same process.
Correct. Each thread has its own execution stack and register context, while sharing the process address space and many process resources.
Open files are generally process-level resources shared by threads, subject to descriptor-level operations.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Operating Systems; processes and threads; Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts, threads.

questions.stem: A user program invokes a protected file-read operation through a system call. What is the essential role of the system-call mechanism?
options: It changes the process permanently into kernel mode
It provides a controlled entry into the kernel so privileged OS services can execute on the program's behalf
It copies the entire disk into user memory before the call
It eliminates the need for access-control checks
explanations: A system call does not permanently leave the process in kernel mode; execution returns to user mode after the service.
Correct. A system call provides a controlled transition to kernel code, where the OS validates arguments and performs privileged operations.
A file-read system call does not copy the entire disk into memory.
The kernel must still enforce permissions and other protection checks.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Operating Systems; system calls, protection and security; Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts, system structures.

questions.stem: A UNIX-like file is assigned permission mode 0754. Which permissions does this encode for owner, group and others, respectively?
options: rwx, r-x, r--
rw-, r-x, rw-
rwx, rw-, r--
r-x, rwx, r--
explanations: Correct. Octal 7=4+2+1 gives rwx; 5=4+1 gives r-x; 4 gives r--.
The owner field is 7, not 6, and others are 4, not 6.
The group field is 5, not 6.
The owner and group permissions are reversed in this option.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Operating Systems; file systems, protection and security; POSIX file permission model / Linux manual pages, chmod.

questions.stem: A disk scheduler repeatedly services the pending request closest to the current head position (Shortest Seek Time First). Which disadvantage can occur under a sustained stream of requests near the current head location?
options: The head must always travel to the physical end before each request
A distant request may be postponed for a long time, causing starvation
The algorithm cannot reduce average seek distance
It guarantees a strict first-come, first-served order
explanations: SSTF does not require movement to the physical end before each request.
Correct. Repeatedly choosing nearby requests can indefinitely postpone a request far from the current head position.
SSTF is used precisely because it can reduce average seek distance compared with FCFS in many workloads.
SSTF does not preserve arrival order; FCFS is the policy that guarantees that order.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Operating Systems; I/O systems and disk scheduling; Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts, mass-storage structure.

questions.stem: In an ER model, a weak entity has a partial key but cannot be uniquely identified by that key alone. How is it normally identified?
options: By its partial key alone across the entire database
By combining the owner's key with the weak entity's partial key
By assigning every attribute a separate primary key
By removing the identifying relationship
explanations: A partial key distinguishes weak entities only within the context of an owner; it is not globally unique by itself.
Correct. A weak entity is identified by the key of its owner entity together with its own partial key.
A separate primary key for every attribute is not the ER identification rule.
The identifying relationship is essential to the weak entity's existence and identification.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Databases; ER model and database design; Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems, ER modelling.

questions.subtopic: Composite B-tree indexes and leftmost-prefix use
questions.stem: A database has a composite B-tree index on columns (city, pincode), in that order. Which query pattern can generally make direct use of the leading index prefix?
options: A predicate on pincode alone, with no condition on city
A predicate on city alone, or on both city and pincode
A predicate only on an unrelated column such as salary
A predicate on the second key only is always as efficient as a predicate on the first key
explanations: A predicate on the second column alone generally cannot exploit the leading-key ordering as a normal prefix lookup.
Correct. A composite index ordered by (city, pincode) can generally support lookups beginning with city, including city alone or city together with pincode.
An unrelated column is not part of this index and cannot be searched directly through it.
The leftmost-prefix property means a predicate on pincode alone is not generally equivalent in efficiency to one on city.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Databases; indexing and query processing; PostgreSQL documentation, multicolumn indexes; https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html

questions.stem: When mapping a binary one-to-many relationship from an ER model to relational tables, where is the foreign key for the relationship normally placed?
options: In the table on the one side, referencing the many-side table
In the table on the many side, referencing the primary key on the one side
In a third table containing one row for every attribute
It is unnecessary because a one-to-many relationship cannot be represented relationally
explanations: Placing the foreign key on the one side would not naturally represent multiple related many-side rows without repeating or restructuring data.
Correct. The primary key of the one-side entity is stored as a foreign key in the relation representing the many-side entity.
A separate table for every attribute is not the standard mapping rule.
A one-to-many relationship is routinely represented using a foreign key.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Databases; ER-to-relational mapping and integrity constraints; Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems, relational database design.

questions.stem: A correlated subquery is used with `WHERE EXISTS (subquery)`. Under SQL semantics, when does EXISTS evaluate to TRUE for a given outer row?
options: When the subquery returns at least one row
Only when the subquery returns exactly one row
Only when the first selected column is non-NULL
When the subquery returns no rows
explanations: Correct. EXISTS tests whether the subquery produces at least one row; the values in its select list do not determine the truth of EXISTS.
EXISTS is true for one or more rows, not only exactly one.
A row containing NULL still counts as a row for EXISTS.
No rows causes EXISTS to be FALSE.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Databases; SQL predicates and subqueries; PostgreSQL documentation, Subquery Expressions – EXISTS; https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-subquery.html

questions.stem: For a PERT activity, the optimistic time is 2 days, the most likely time is 5 days and the pessimistic time is 8 days. Using the standard three-point PERT estimate, what is the expected duration?
options: 4 days
5 days
5.5 days
6 days
explanations: Four days is below the weighted estimate.
Correct. Expected duration = (a+4m+b)/6 = (2+4×5+8)/6 = 30/6 = 5 days.
5.5 days is not the result of the standard PERT weighting.
Six days would be the simple average of the three estimates, not the weighted PERT estimate.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Information Systems and Software Engineering; project planning and management; standard PERT three-point estimate, e.g. Pressman, Software Engineering.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes beta testing from alpha testing in software development?
options: Beta testing is always performed by the development team in a controlled laboratory
Beta testing is typically performed by selected external users in a real or realistic user environment before general release
Alpha testing can begin only after public release
Alpha and beta testing are both forms of static code inspection
explanations: The development team in a controlled environment is more characteristic of alpha testing.
Correct. Beta testing involves selected users outside the development organisation using the product in realistic conditions before wider release.
Alpha testing generally occurs before beta testing and before public release.
Both alpha and beta are execution-based testing activities, not static code inspection.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Information Systems and Software Engineering; testing and implementation; Pressman and Maxim, Software Engineering: A Practitioner's Approach, software testing.

questions.stem: A deployed billing system produces an incorrect tax total because of a defect in its calculation routine. A patch is issued to remove that defect. What type of software maintenance is this?
options: Adaptive maintenance
Perfective maintenance
Corrective maintenance
Preventive maintenance
explanations: Adaptive maintenance changes software to accommodate a changed environment or platform.
Perfective maintenance improves performance, maintainability or functionality beyond correcting a fault.
Correct. Corrective maintenance fixes faults discovered after delivery.
Preventive maintenance modifies software to reduce the likelihood of future problems, rather than directly correcting this reported defect.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Information Systems and Software Engineering; software life cycle, implementation and maintenance; ISO/IEC/IEEE 14764, Software Life Cycle Processes – Maintenance.

questions.stem: A router has two matching routes for destination 10.1.2.77: 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.1.2.0/24. Which route is selected by standard longest-prefix matching?
options: 10.1.0.0/16 because it was learned first
10.1.2.0/24 because it has the longer matching prefix
Both routes are used in alternating packets by default
The router must discard the packet because two routes match
explanations: Route age is not the general selection rule when longest-prefix matching applies.
Correct. The /24 route matches more leading address bits than /16 and is therefore the most specific route.
Equal-cost multipath requires equal preference and prefix length or other routing conditions; it is not the default result here.
Multiple matching prefixes are normal in routing tables; the most specific matching route is selected.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Networks; routing algorithms and IPv4 forwarding; RFC 1812, Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers; https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812

questions.subtopic: IPv4 TTL and ICMP Time Exceeded
questions.stem: An IPv4 packet reaches a router with TTL=1. What should a conforming router do when forwarding the packet would reduce the TTL to zero?
options: Forward it with TTL=0
Discard it and normally send an ICMP Time Exceeded message, subject to ICMP error-message rules
Reset the TTL to 64
Fragment it into two packets
explanations: An IPv4 packet with TTL reduced to zero must not be forwarded.
Correct. The router discards the packet and normally reports ICMP Time Exceeded, subject to the protocol's restrictions on generating ICMP errors.
Routers do not reset an expired packet's TTL to 64.
TTL expiration is unrelated to fragmentation; the router does not split the packet for this reason.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Networks; IPv4 and ICMP; RFC 791 and RFC 792; https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc791 and https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc792

questions.stem: In a typical authenticated TLS connection, what is the primary purpose of the server's certificate chain?
options: To encrypt all application data directly with the certificate's public key
To bind the server's identity to a public key through signatures that the client can validate to a trusted root
To assign the client's IP address dynamically
To replace the need for a key exchange
explanations: Application data is normally protected with negotiated symmetric traffic keys, not encrypted directly with the certificate public key.
Correct. The certificate chain lets the client validate that a trusted certificate authority has vouched for the association between the server identity and its public key.
IP address assignment is the role of network configuration protocols such as DHCP.
A certificate authenticates a public key; it does not by itself replace the TLS key-establishment process.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Networks; public-key cryptography and secure protocols; RFC 8446, TLS 1.3; https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446

questions.stem: For UDP over IPv4, which information is included in the pseudo-header used in checksum computation in addition to the UDP header and data?
options: Source IP address, destination IP address, protocol number and UDP length
Only the source and destination MAC addresses
The complete Ethernet frame including its FCS
Only the destination IP address and application port
explanations: Correct. The IPv4 pseudo-header includes source and destination IP addresses, a zero field, protocol number and UDP length, helping detect misdelivery to the wrong IP protocol or addresses.
MAC addresses belong to the link layer and are not part of the UDP pseudo-header.
The Ethernet frame and its FCS are outside UDP checksum computation.
The pseudo-header includes both IP addresses, protocol identification and UDP length, not only the destination address and port.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Networks; TCP/UDP and transport-layer error detection; RFC 768, User Datagram Protocol; https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc768

questions.stem: In XML, two elements use different prefixes, but both prefixes are bound to the same namespace URI and the elements have the same local name. How are their expanded names treated?
options: As different names because the prefixes differ
As the same expanded name because the namespace URI and local name match
As invalid XML because one URI cannot have two prefixes
As the same name only if the prefixes are lexically identical
explanations: A prefix is a placeholder and is not itself part of the expanded name.
Correct. An expanded name is determined by the namespace URI and local part; different prefixes bound to the same URI can identify the same expanded name.
XML permits multiple prefixes to be bound to the same namespace URI.
Lexical prefix identity is not required when the namespace URI and local name are identical.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; XML namespaces; W3C Namespaces in XML 1.0 Recommendation; https://www.w3.org/TR/xml-names/

questions.stem: In PHP, for a variable `$x` that is set to the integer value `0`, which statement is correct?
options: isset($x) is false and empty($x) is false
isset($x) is true and empty($x) is true
isset($x) is true and empty($x) is false
Both isset($x) and empty($x) are false
explanations: `isset` is true for a variable set to zero, so this option is false.
Correct. `isset($x)` is true because x exists and is not NULL; `empty($x)` is also true because zero is treated as empty in PHP.
`empty(0)` evaluates to true in PHP, so the second part of this option is false.
Both expressions are not false; isset is true for a set, non-NULL variable.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; PHP; PHP Manual, isset() and empty(); https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.isset.php and https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.empty.php

questions.stem: A JavaScript function is returned from an outer function and invoked after the outer function has finished executing. Why can it still access a local variable declared in the outer function?
options: The browser automatically copies every local variable into the global object
The returned function retains access to its lexical environment through a closure
JavaScript restarts the outer function whenever the inner function is called
The variable is converted automatically into a DOM property
explanations: Ordinary local variables are not automatically copied to the global object.
Correct. A closure retains the lexical environment needed to resolve free variables even after the outer call has returned.
Calling the inner function does not restart the outer function.
Lexical variables do not become DOM properties merely because a function is returned.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; client-side scripting; ECMAScript Language Specification, Environment Records and closures; https://tc39.es/ecma262/

questions.topic: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA
questions.stem: A Java try-with-resources statement declares resources R1 and then R2. If both resources are successfully initialized and the statement exits, in what order are they closed?
options: R1, then R2
R2, then R1
In parallel, with no specified order
Only R2 is closed automatically
explanations: Resources are not closed in declaration order.
Correct. Java closes resources in the reverse order of their initialization/declaration, so R2 closes before R1.
The language specifies reverse-order closing; it is not an unspecified parallel operation.
Both resources are closed automatically when control leaves the try-with-resources statement.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA; Java Language Specification, try-with-resources; https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/

questions.topic: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA
questions.stem: Which property of a built-in C++ operator cannot be changed by overloading that operator for a user-defined type?
options: The implementation body executed for the user-defined operands
The operator's precedence and associativity
The return type of the overloaded function
The class in which a member overload is declared
explanations: The programmer supplies the overloaded operator's implementation body.
Correct. Overloading cannot change an operator's precedence, associativity or number of operands; those are fixed by the language grammar.
An overloaded operator function may have an appropriate user-defined return type.
A member overload can be declared in the class, subject to the language's operator-overloading rules.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA; ISO C++ standard, operator overloading; https://eel.is/c++draft/over.oper

questions.topic: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA
questions.stem: A class implements interface I, which declares a static method `helper()`. How is that interface static method normally invoked?
options: Through an instance of the implementing class, using dynamic dispatch
Through the interface name, such as I.helper()
It is automatically inherited as a static method of every implementing class
Only from within a constructor of the implementing class
explanations: Interface static methods are not instance methods and are not dynamically dispatched through an implementing object.
Correct. A static method declared in an interface is invoked using the interface type name.
Interface static methods are not inherited by implementing classes as their own static methods.
The method is not restricted to constructors; it can be invoked through the interface name wherever accessible.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA; Java Language Specification, interface methods; https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/

questions.stem: Why does the gain-ratio criterion divide information gain by split information when selecting an attribute for a decision tree?
options: To favour attributes with the largest number of distinct values even more strongly
To reduce information gain's bias toward attributes that create many small partitions
To make every split have exactly zero entropy
To replace class labels with continuous target values
explanations: Gain ratio is intended to reduce, not amplify, the preference for attributes with many distinct values.
Correct. Split information normalises information gain and can penalise attributes that fragment the data into many partitions.
The criterion does not force child nodes or splits to have zero entropy.
Gain ratio is a classification split criterion and does not convert a categorical target into a continuous one.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; classification algorithms and decision-tree induction; Quinlan, C4.5: Programs for Machine Learning, gain ratio.

questions.stem: A random forest is trained using bootstrap samples of size n drawn with replacement from n training cases. Approximately what fraction of the original cases is left out of a particular tree's bootstrap sample as out-of-bag data for large n?
options: About 5%
About 18.4%
About 36.8%
About 63.2%
explanations: About 5% is too small; repeated sampling with replacement leaves a much larger fraction unselected.
About 18.4% is not the limiting probability of being unselected.
Correct. The probability a case is never selected is (1−1/n)ⁿ, which approaches e⁻¹≈0.368 as n grows.
About 63.2% is the approximate fraction selected at least once, not the out-of-bag fraction.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; classification ensembles and random forests; Breiman, Random Forests (2001), bootstrap sampling and out-of-bag estimation.

questions.stem: A one-versus-rest strategy is used to extend a binary classifier to K mutually exclusive classes. How many binary classifiers are trained?
options: K
2K
explanations: K−1 is not the standard one-versus-rest count; that count belongs to some other multiclass decompositions.
Correct. One classifier is trained for each class, treating that class as positive and all remaining classes as negative.
K(K−1)/2 is the number of pairwise classifiers in one-versus-one classification.
2K is not the one-versus-rest classifier count.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; classification algorithms; standard one-versus-rest multiclass reduction, scikit-learn User Guide; https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/multiclass.html

questions.stem: A binary classifier produces a score interpreted as the probability of the positive class. If the positive-class decision threshold is lowered while the score distribution is unchanged, which effect is generally expected?
options: Fewer cases are predicted positive, so sensitivity generally falls
More cases are predicted positive, so sensitivity generally rises and specificity may fall
Both sensitivity and specificity must rise
The ROC curve becomes undefined
explanations: Lowering the threshold generally classifies more cases as positive, not fewer.
Correct. A lower threshold tends to increase true positives and sensitivity/recall, while it can also increase false positives and reduce specificity.
Sensitivity and specificity generally trade off as the threshold changes; they do not both have to rise.
The ROC curve is defined from true-positive and false-positive rates across thresholds.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; classification evaluation and decision thresholds; standard classification metrics, scikit-learn User Guide; https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html

questions.stem: In permutation feature importance, how is the importance of a feature commonly estimated on a validation set?
options: By measuring the score change after randomly permuting that feature's values while leaving other features unchanged
By counting the number of times the feature name appears in the source code
By assigning the feature the largest possible numeric value
By removing the target variable before training and measuring training accuracy
explanations: Correct. Permutation importance measures how much model performance deteriorates when the association between one feature and the target is broken by permuting that feature.
Source-code frequency is unrelated to predictive contribution.
Setting a feature to a large value is not the permutation procedure and may create out-of-distribution data.
Removing the target variable would prevent supervised training rather than estimate feature importance.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; classification evaluation and feature relevance; scikit-learn User Guide, permutation feature importance; https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/permutation_importance.html
